title: Efficient Selectivity and Backup Operators in Monte-Carlo Tree Search
headline: Grow a game tree one random playout at a time, steer each playout toward the move most likely to be best so you never fully give up on anything, and read each node's value as a blend that slides from the average toward the best as the playouts pile up.
abstract: Monte-Carlo evaluation consists in estimating a position by averaging the outcome of several random continuations, and can serve as an evaluation function at the leaves of a min-max tree. This paper presents a new framework to combine tree search with Monte-Carlo evaluation, that does not separate between a min-max phase and a Monte-Carlo phase. Instead of backing-up the min-max value close to the root, and the average value at some depth, a more general backup operator is defined that progressively changes from averaging to min-max as the number of simulations grows. This approach provides a fine-grained control of the tree growth, at the level of individual simulations, and allows efficient selectivity methods. This algorithm was implemented in a 9 x 9 Go-playing program, Crazy Stone, that won the 10th KGS computer-Go tournament.

source.name: 5th International Conference on Computers and Games 2006

images.alt: A small pixel-art tree of nodes grows from a root at the top, with one clay-orange path lit from the root down to a single leaf and a thin ink arrow curling back up the same path, while the other branches stay sage green, showing that the search grows one random playout at a time by descending to a promising leaf and carrying the result back up.
images.caption: Each playout descends from the root to a leaf, runs a random game, and carries the result back up the path it walked.

images.alt: Three pixel-art dig sites in a row, two shallow sage holes with a few pebbles and one deeper hole with a glowing clay-orange gem half-buried in dirt, with ink arrows still sending probes into the gem hole, showing that a good move can look bad at first so the search keeps probing it instead of giving up.
images.caption: A good move can look bad early, so the search keeps probing every move and never cuts one off completely.

images.alt: A hand-inked dial labelled value sits between a pixel-art scale weighing pebbles on the left, labelled average, and a glowing clay-orange gem on a pedestal on the right, labelled best, with the pointer sliding toward the gem, showing that a node's backed-up value starts as the average of its playouts and slides toward the best one as more playouts arrive.
images.caption: A node's value starts as the average of its playouts and slides toward the best child as the playout count grows.

images.alt: A pixel-art hatchet chops through a green branch marked pruned while a glowing clay-orange gem hangs on that very branch, about to fall away, showing that cutting off a move on a few unlucky early playouts can throw away the move that was secretly best.
images.caption: Cutting a move on a few unlucky early playouts can throw away the move that was secretly best.
